summary:
Jujuy stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action that applies to Jujuy as to every province. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported the ban on surgery and hormone treatment for adolescents; legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, already common nationally, has worsened since the current national administration took office. An April 2025 Washington Blade report datelined Buenos Aires places the worst of it outside Buenos Aires and names Jujuy among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is even more so.

Violence nationally reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a ten-year record and a 62% rise year on year, averaging one every 38 hours. Security-force personnel were among the most frequent perpetrators, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons.
tangentialFactors:
Agencia Presentes, reporting the 2025 hate-crime figures on 19 March 2026, identifies beatings as the main modality of attack, records institutional violence rising from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and finds that 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims. Agencia Presentes described the annual total as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-state organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jujuy are affected by the dismissal of trans people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota and by the abolition of the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI, both reported in April 2025, which removes the national body that handled discrimination complaints.

The second February 2025 decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons applies to trans detainees held in Jujuy's prison system, where 32% of nationally recorded 2025 hate-crime incidents occurred in police stations or prisons.

Jujuy has no local reporting infrastructure of its own to generate separate hate-crime records, so residents' exposure to violence is captured only in the national observatory's totals.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Jujuy-specific incident record, provincial statute on gender markers, facilities access or hate-crime reporting scheme is sourced in the inventory; the province's position is established by the application of national law and by the Washington Blade's naming of Jujuy among the provinces where police violence is worst.

Whether the February 2025 decrees survive judicial challenge is unresolved: legal experts have stated an intention to seek judicial intervention, and no outcome is sourced.

The extent to which Jujuy's own anti-discrimination provisions operate independently of the abolished federal agency is not sourced and remains unresolved.
